speechtext: I am pleased to inform hon. members of the promotion to the position of Second Clerk Assistant of the House of Commons of Mr. Alexander Small. Mr. Small will continue to serve as Director of Legislative Services. I am sure hon. members will be gratified at this recognition of the services of this loyal, competent and highly esteemed table officer.

subtopic: MR. STEWART (COCHRANE)-PROCEDURE FOR DEALING WITH PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
MR. STEWART (COCHRANE)-PROCEDURE FOR DEALING WITH PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects me personally and the principle of which affects all hon. members who are considered as backbenchers. Yesterday an announcement was made by the Department of Finance that effigies of former Prime Ministers would be placed on Canadian currency. This is a measure which I welcome, but it is one which I introduced in the form of a private member's bill during the last session on February 6, 1969, as found on page 5213 of Hansard. That private member's bill has been sitting on the Order Paper for almost one year and now a decision by a department of government puts into effect the subject matter of that bill without referring to it.
All hon. members are encouraged to take an active part in government and to bring forth new ideas. However, the system used according to the rules of the House to deal with private members' bills is such that backbenchers do not have sufficient opportunity to participate in the way they should.
To illustrate how the detail of the announcement coincides with what I did last February, let me say that after introducing my bill I outlined some suggestions for dealing with it, such as keeping the effigy of Her Majesty on one of the denominations. I even
ventured an opinion, wrongly as it turns out, that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) would not comment on it because he would be torn between two great loves. However, the bill has never had the opportunity to come before the House because of a silly method for determining the business of private members.

Before the second session began all of the bills were thrown together and drawn from a hat in order to determine their precedence. It seems to me that legislation should not be considered as a matter of chance. When a member waits for a long list of bills to be disposed of throughout one session he should not be obliged to wait for another list to be disposed of in a new session before being able to deal with his bill. When a member suggests a piece of legislation which is adopted by the government almost one year later, should he not be entitled to at least a teeny bit of recognition?
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy):
That the matter of dealing more efficiently with private members' business be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister without Portfolio):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after personal meetings and discussions with the responsible ministers from the provinces I announced on August 14 that:
Until a more well defined and logical longterm Canadian urban renewal policy can be formulated and enunciated, municipalities with urban renewal schemes presently in preparation will have to elect either to suspend further study or, alternatively, to complete their work in the knowledge that additional federal funds for implementation of the schemes may or may not be forthcoming.
At that time, also, I approved six projects and authorized negotiation for limited participation in six more. Shortly following that action, all municipalities preparing urban renewal schemes were informed of this announcement by letter.
More recently, Monday, December 8, I informed hon. members in the House that we have launched a full inquiry into the whole process of urbanization in an attempt to establish a set of rational objectives and a co-ordinated policy and program framework at the federal level, involving consultations with provincial governments and other interested parties. Our basic concern is to see that the causes and not just the symptoms are dealt with and that existing or proposed new interventions are related and productive. The urban renewal program, as administered under the National Housing Act-1964 amendment-is but one small component of the broad and complex process of urban redevelopment. Urban growth reflects the actions of
2119
Housing and Urban Renewal three levels of government and numerous private market forces; yet this one intervention-urban renewal-particularly, has not been linked with these other actions.
The program is an extremely rigid instrument. It is rigid in its requirement for a three-stage process-study, scheme, implementation-and in the resulting commitment to action in a tightly designated small section of a city. The process is tortuously long, resulting too often in stagnation and, in its final focus, removing the flexibility of a municipality-for example, in applying resources to a series of perhaps dispersed but planned interventions for clearance, rehabilitation and redevelopment.
Moreover, in the absence of clearly defined economic and social goals, including the provision of housing for the most disadvantaged income groups, the program appears to have served a multitude of often contradictory purposes which were never foreseen in the original definition. For example, as a result of urban renewal activities to date, there has been a net loss in low income housing stock.
As I said on December 8, we are embarked upon a deep study of the urban process- identification of the determinants of urban growth, the causes of urban problems, the inter-relationship of governmental action at and between each level, and the other forces at work. At this stage, I admit quite freely that we are impressed mainly by the complexity of the social systems that cities have become. The finding of solutions will be a major undertaking involving much expertise, all governments and the public-consultations which we will seek and welcome.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
In the meantime we do not see the wisdom or justification for an expansion of government intervention, of major new dimensions, in programs such as urban renewal, some forms of which are doubtful in their results. We see rather a need for more emphasis on low income housing and such investments that provide clear and more immediate benefits.
If, Mr. Speaker, I accepted only those urban renewal schemes about to be brought to the implementation stage, the federal treasury alone would be involved in ultimate expenditures approaching $400 million and loans up to two-thirds of the total grant. Provincial and municipal expenditures would have been on a similar scale. No rationale could be
2120	COMMONS
Housing and Urban Renewal devised to support an immediate decision to commit such a level of expenditure when so little is lost in this pause until a sounder basis is provided.
Having said that, however, I should note that even in this transitional stage, Mr. Speaker, there are some schemes to which all three levels of government have an identifiable commitment and which, in our view, can be accepted within the general concerns I have expressed. Over and above the six on which negotiations started in August, there are 12 such projects distributed between the eight provinces of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.
Within specific dollar amounts in each case,
I am offering to the provincial ministers responsible and have authorized CMHC officials to proceed with negotiations toward at least partial implementation of these additional 12 projects. To fund the federal grant share of these and other approvals up to and including this year, federal expenditures for this program will be maintained at a level of approximately $25 million annually for the five-year period 1970 through 1974.
That is a big deal.

This compares with expenditures of $7.5 million in 1967, $12.5 million in 1968, and $23 million in 1969. Beyond that, further investments in urban renewal are most unlikely at least until the urban policy review is completed next year, and it is quite possible that the results of that review will indicate the need for new directions and programs of urban assistance.
For those communities with schemes in preparation but not ready or not approved, I have asked my officials to re-examine each project in order to determine whether some of the work they wish to do can be accomplished by other NHA programs-land assembly, section 16 or section 40 loans, public housing, sewage treatment loans-or whether they can be assisted by other federal departmental programs. Some municipalities have already begun to negotiate redevelopment with private sources-I understand with some reason for optimism-and others may wish to do the same, based upon the schemes prepared. Should communities wish to de-designate the areas set aside for urban renewal, we shall certainly honour our commitment to contribute to the cost of the scheme preparation completed to that date.

DEBATES	December 18, 1963
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that inherent in this approach I have outlined is a principle to which I subscribe, that of the need for constant program evaluation. Even the most well intentioned plan conceived can encounter unforseen weaknesses and changing priorities and conditions when executed. Failure to undertake critical evaluation as a constant requirement so that these weaknesses are identified, or failure to adjust to the need for change, even though inconvenient and sometimes painful, leads to the waste of scarce resources and would be irresponsible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There is not much enthusiasm in that statement.
Mr. Speaker, at long last the Minister without Portfolio responsible for housing has made a statement on urban renewal. But his statement says nothing.
Hear, hear.
It is nothing but a slap in the face for the cities.
Hear, hear.

On the basis of the statement, I submit it is clear that the government is not giving leadership in this area. It ought to give more leadership and ought to make sure that the three levels of government confer with a view to solving the problems that beset our urban centres. What concerns me more than anything is that the cities have difficulty in gaining the ear of the government. I hope the minister will, in his sincerity, support the proposition that this party has recently stated in terms of so structuring the parliamentary committee on the constitution that we will be able to have dialogue, consultation and direction from the cities. Perhaps here we will get the answers.
Urban renewal is a fact. I am surprised the minister did not state it is not the fault of the cities that they have so obviously gotten into this mess but rather the fault of this government and its bureaucracy for entering into programs without giving them any study whatsoever.
Hear, hear!

The former minister in charge of housing indicated, when he suddenly realized what was happening, that he had found out it would take 120 years before we
December 18, 1969
would be able to pay for the renewal schemes that are on the boards. He also said he had great sympathy with the cities which had thought the money would be available. This is the point, Mr. Speaker. It is the fault of this government rather than the cities with respect to their plans for urban renewal.
The minister indicated there would be $25 million per year available between 1970 and 1974. This is an illogical statement, Mr. Speaker, when we think of all the money that has been spent-$125 million wiped out with respect to Expo, the cost of the art centre jumping from $9 million to $46 million and on the CBC, which is questionable in many respects, some $200 million. In addition, recently the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) approved construction of a $28 million departmental building. If we are talking in terms of money, Mr. Speaker, where is the rationale with respect to the minister's statement?
The city of Hamilton-and when I say this I speak on behalf of all cities-is looking for leadership and guidance in this area. They are going to be very disappointed and dismayed. The minister mentioned money in his statement. We do not know yet how much money will be available for each city. I know the city of Hamilton was supposed to receive a $5 million federal contribution and only received approximately $2 million. Is the minister, through this program, going to give the city of Hamilton another $2J million?
I am pleased the minister mentioned public housing. The Hon. Stanley J. Randall, speaking on behalf of Ontario, and I am sure this applies to other provinces as well, stated:
To date, the federal guidelines on public housing have not been established and this is making itself felt in large areas like metropolitan Toronto where uncertainty over size and design is affecting planning for further projects.
The Canadian Welfare Council has stated that we require 30,000 public housing units per year. I wonder how much of the government's program for one million units is going to be geared to actual public housing? I do not have the figures for 1969 but in 1968 there were only 13,527 such units constructed.
In conclusion I wish to say I am ashamed that the minister has not brought out his guidelines on public housing. As a matter of fact, he has not brought out guidelines on anything.

Hear, hear.

The minister indicated he would give us guidelines for urban renewal and public housing. In the long run, he has not given us any guidelines at all. All he has given us is the same story that he has been telling for some time. I wonder whether the minister cannot make a statement on guidelines for urban renewal because this government is studying the constitutional problems as they affect the cities. I understand there is a problem among the government frontbenchers as to what role the federal government will play. Perhaps we will have to wait until the government makes up its mind as to the role it can play in solving urban problems before it definitely decides what it is going to do with respect to urban renewal.

Mr. Speaker, after hearing the statement by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras), is it any wonder the former minister in charge of housing, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), resigned? I should like to preface my remarks by saying that the minister now in charge of housing is a very able, sincere and concerned person. He possessed these qualities when he was involved in Indian affairs but when he began to demand action to bring about a better deal for the Indians he was quickly shunted out because his ideas were not those of the government.
We now find him in exactly the same position with regard to housing. His ideas are not those of the government or, especially, of the Prime Minister who does not believe in active federal participation in housing. This is why the minister had to content himself with such statements as "we must await a better defined long term Canadian urban renewal policy", and that he is deeply impressed by the complexity of the problem. Mr. Speaker, the failure to produce urban renewal policies can be placed squarely on the present government for its lack of leadership and initiative in this field.
Between 1946 and 1969 hon. gentlemen opposite have spent a mere $186 million on urban renewal and have erected a Berlin wall of obstruction and frustration in the way of its success. In 1964, when the amendments to the National Housing Act with respect to the financing of urban renewal were passed, they were put into effect in three stages. Assistance was promised in the financing of studies undertaken by municipalities in the area of urban renewal schemes.

December 18, 1969

Housing and Urban Renewal Experience showed, however, that many municipalities had neither the money nor the planning staffs to make this scheme a success. Therefore in 1967 the government proposed amendments to the act and from 1967 to the present time no initiative has been taken in this field even though cabinet approval was given. As to the second phase, assistance in the preparation of schemes, the municipalities were required to make a financial contribution amounting to 50 per cent, a demand which imposed further hardship on them.
The third stage of the implementation of the scheme turned out to be a real failure. Not only did the government impose a 50 per cent financial contribution but no provision was made in legislation or otherwise in connection with the setting up of schools, recreational centres, day care centres and the like. In addition, the expropriation laws prevailing at that time worked severe hardship on those who had to deal with urban renewal. Again, zoning regulations and tax structures further hampered any real development in the field.
When the hon. member for Trinity, the integrated one-man band in the housing field, set forth in his task force report the notion that urban renewal and public housing were the areas of failure, making them the whipping boys, he did a great disservice to Canada. Since that time there has been a freeze on housing and urban renewal; only a slight thaw has been noticeable on the part of the minister presently in charge of housing. Is it any wonder he is only perpetuating the failure of the government in the field of urban renewal?
We in the New Democratic Party believe there should be active participation and partnership among the three levels of government together with all others involved in urban renewal. We ask the minister to call an immediate conference of all departments and agencies of government which are concerned in this matter. Second, we call for active federal leadership and initiative in helping to solve the problems of urban renewal. We heard the minister say he is making an allocation of a mere $25 million a year toward urban renewal. This is a serious disappointment to us. We ask for further financial assistance in this area so that the municipalities and provincial governments can play a more active part in attacking one of the main causes of the difficulties which beset our cities today. We in the NDP are greatly disappointed in the minister's statement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' PUBLIC BILLS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask the unanimous consent of the House under Standing Order 43 to move a motion which I shall place before you in a few moments. I may say as evidence of the urgency attached to this request that I decided to seek consent to this motion only after hearing the hon. member for Cochrane speak this afternoon.
The present Standing Orders in relation to private members' bills are part hypocrisy and part stupidity. I feel that private members should at the earliest opportunity be provided with a better method of putting forward their public bills. Therefore I ask the consent of the House to move the following motion:
That the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization review Standing Orders dealing with Private Members' Public Bills with a view to making a report to the House with a recommendation that changes be made including the right to allow a recorded vote on some of such bills.
As further evidence of urgency may I say that this motion closely parallels a motion which appears in my name under private members' motions as No. 39, and that I am foregoing my right to make a speech on it by putting forward at this time the motion which I have just read.

The House resumed from Wednesday, December 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-139, to amend an act to amend the Income Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to the Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to oppose the proposal of the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray).
I feel it is my duty to voice the views and aspirations of my fellow citizens regarding this motion but I will be brief.
The purpose of Bill C-139 before us is to extend for another year the imposition of the 3 per cent surtax. I would like to comment on the statement made during the last session by the Minister without Portfolio when he first introduced a bill to impose a 3 per cent surtax on personal income, as reported on page 9417 of Hansard for June 3 last. The minister used these very words:
In making this proposal tonight, I am mindful of the implication given last October that these surtaxes would be allowed to terminate as scheduled and that this was a factor in determining the series of tax measures then introduced. It will be clear to everyone, however, that the extension of the surtaxes at this time is required for the purposes of economic stabilization, and not for budgetary revenues.
It is clear that the legislation brought before us by the minister without portfolio is not based on an urgent need to supply the government with more money so that it may meet its commitments. As the minister said, it is a mere question of stabilizing the Canadian economy.
This 3 per cent surtax which has been suggested on a temporary basis represents a very strange Christmas gift to Canadians, who thought that it would affect them for one year only. So, they are being offered a very strange gift, that is a surtax they will have to pay for at least another year.
As the minister refuses to promise the withdrawal of this surtax at the end of another year, we are justified in believing that it will become permanent.
I just had to take a few seconds to say that the workers in my constituency and in others as well are unfairly subjected to that tax, for
Income Tax Act
it contributes to maintaining the cost of living at a high level and to perpetuating inflation. This is a glaring injustice, especially for low or middle income workers.
Through that surtax the government does not have to levy, according to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), the latter will dig into the pockets of the workers for the money they would need to meet their obligations. He will collect, in the coming year, the neat little sum of $20 million or so.
One does not have to give it much thought to blame severely the minister and the government for not being able to meet their obligations, and for levying a useless surtax.
As I said a while ago, that 3 per cent surtax was first levied on a temporary basis, but it is becoming permanent. We must also remember that this surtax was born in the month of February 1968, when the government proposed a 5 per cent surtax and was defeated in the House. The Canadians who, at the time, blamed the government and hoped to have the opportunity of telling it that they had enough of that Liberal administration, were forced to put up with its incompetence and finally ended up with a surtax no one wants.
Under the circumstances, we therefore have no choice. Indeed, we must vote against this surtax and ask the government to quit oppressing the low income workers. Those who are responsible for administrating public affairs, must, at long last, assume their responsibilities and respect the promises they made during the election campaign by drawing closer to the needs of the people. Only then will they understand that it is imperative for them to stop oppressing the Canadian workers, and to discontinue levying this 3 per cent surtax.
Hear, hear.

May I say a few words about this taxation bill, Mr. Speaker? The other day the Minister without Portfolio from Windsor West (Mr. Gray) suggested that this measure has been introduced in order that we may cool inflation. I read his remarks again just now, and that clearly is the inference to be drawn from them. I suggest that not all parts of the country are contributing to inflation and for that reason the government ought to consider introducing other measures to deal with existing problems. You know, Mr. Speaker, when other people lose their jobs we call it a reces-

December 18, 1989
Income Tax Act
sion; but when we lose our own jobs, then we call it a depression. Passage of this bill will adversely affect all those who are in economic difficulties and will do nothing to solve the problems of certain parts of the country. Of course, I am talking mainly about western Canada, because I know that part of the country. But my remarks apply equally to other, less prosperous parts of the country.
The minister may say that the economy needs cooling; but it does not need cooling right across Canada. The government ought to consider introducing fiscal policies which would help certain disadvantaged parts of the country and consider pumping more money into those areas. The government ought to consider industries in this country on a regional basis. For instance, if the potash industry is in trouble, it ought to consider helping that industry. If the oil industry or the agricultural industry is in trouble, the minister ought to consider helping those industries by implementing helpful fiscal policies. Although we have introduced fiscal measures involving tariffs, I notice that the tariffs do not work equally for the benefit of all parts of the country. For example, tariffs on automobile products affect mainly that small portion of the country encompassing the Windsor area, Toronto, and the Oshawa area. The people living in those areas might object violently if we were to tamper with automobile tariffs, yet hon. members representing those areas of the country will do little to reciprocate and help other parts of the country. Clearly, since the automobile industry and other similar industries are fairly affluent, it may make sense for us to say that we ought to cool the economy so far as those industries are concerned. But we should not apply such cooling measures right across the board. Certain industries need to be helped, and for that reason the government ought not to use a blanket approach in attempting to solve problems.
This bill reminds me of a Jerry-built house. I once saw a house that had attached to it a lean-to; another lean-to was added to the first one, and still another lean-to had been added to the second. This legislation reminds me of that structure, because it symbolizes this government's approach to taxation. If the government could assure us that in its tax reform proposals there would be changes in the kind of tax it is now seeking to impose, we might be more ready to listen to the government. Unfortunately there is no such
fMr. Thomson.]
assurance. Apparently the surtax is to be dealt with as the CNR indebtedness is dealt with, that is every year. We were told at one time that this would be a special tax. I submit that it is not solving our problems. I urge the minister from Windsor West not to cool the economy of the country right across the board, because some areas of the country need help if they are to solve some of their problems. If adequate fiscal measures are introduced to help those areas of the country, we shall be helping the economy generally and thereby bring about some semblance of unity which has real meaning within Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would not speak again to the main motion at this stage were it not for the seriousness of the situation we are facing at the present time. I think the government has to consider very seriously the question of its credibility and the confidence which the people of Canada will have in it, in view of developments which have taken place over the past several months and in view of the increasing feeling that the government has lost control of the situation and is no longer capable of grasping the problems we are confronted with in Canada. In considering this bill I think we have to keep in mind the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) last June when he delivered his budget speech. As has been pointed out previously, he said, as reported at page 9417 of Hansard:
It will be clear to everyone, however, that the extension of the surtaxes at this time is required for the purposes of economic stabilization, and not for budgetary revenues.
We must take a look at the performance of the economy since that time, at what public attitudes today are and at the public's response to government policies.
I note with considerable interest an article in this morning's Globe and Mail written by George Bain which, it seems to me, sums up pretty well public feeling at present towards the government's so-called policies of economic stabilization, of which this bill forms a part, as the minister has said. May I through you, Mr. Speaker, draw to the attention of hon. members part of what Mr. Bain wrote in this morning's Globe and Mail article. The article reads:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This Government has Its moments when it sinks into a state of absolutely numb fatheadedness-as, for particular example, when Finance Minister
December 18, 1969

Edgar Benson was asked by Robert Stanfield the other day what he intends to do about the continuing rise in the cost of living.
If there is one subject on which the Government ought to do its best to cultivate the appearance of humility, it's that one; there's nothing in the record to be self-satisfied about.
Ministers themselves, Mr. Benson among them, have been prating for months about the further remedies they hold in reserve, and with the cost-of-living index having reached 127.4 with no sign that it will stop there, a certain curiosity about what those measures are and when they are likely to be employed shouldn't be altogether surprising.
He goes on to mention some of the statements that were made by the Minister of Finance when he delivered his budget speech last June. At this time, I suggest the government should seriously consider withdrawing the bill. I think many Canadians would, in fact regard it as something of a Christmas present to the economy if the government saw fit to withdraw this bill. It certainly would be more in keeping with new economic trends that have developed since the Minister of Finance delivered his budget speech.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, the Minister without Portfolio, when he concludes the debate, will give some indication that the government is in fact having second thoughts about this policy and will consider withdrawing this bill at this time.

speechtext: Is the House ready for the question? The hon. member for Compton.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on Bill C-139, an untimely measure to introduce in the House.
No later than yesterday, we were given some proof of that when the minister was asked a question and we were told that the government does not need the money because it collects other taxes. Some public works and other projects have been stopped in order to save money and balance the government budget.
The 3 per cent surtax had been imposed for a year, and the government had suggested that it would disappear once the budget had been stabilized. But now, we are asked to maintain that harmful and untimely surtax.
Yesterday, I asked the minister the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister why the government is maintaining this tax. We are told that for 1970, the government is expecting a huge surplus.
Income Tax Act
If the budget of the government is satisfactorily balanced, why should it unbalance the budgets of all Canadians to the benefit of the federal government's?
The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray) answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said, in his budget speech, that it was necessary, in order to win the battle against inflation, to maintain fiscal restraints. In this regard, one of the methods he advocated was to maintain the surtax for one year in order to win this battle against inflation, which is in the interest of all Canadians, including the lower income groups.
Considering this answer, I wonder what proportion of the population will be paying this tax. The statement that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) made yesterday was absolutely correct. This is what he said:
Even though the subsequent measure, an extension of which we are now debating, levied a 3 per cent tax on individual income and corporations as well, it is still grossly unfair. If this bill is passed, in 1970 the government will collect an additional $115 million from the individual income tax payer and only $40 million from corporations. This is a ratio of 3 to 1, that is $3 from the average, medium and low income taxpayers in Canada and $1 from corporations.
In the remainder of this year, an additional $25 million will be collected, $20 million from individuals and $5 million from corporations.
This is a ratio of 4 to 1, $4 being collected from individuals and $1 from corporations. The total tax revenue forecast for 1969-70 is on a ratio much closer to 2 to 1, that is $2 from individuals and $1 from corporations. Because of these figures I just quoted, surely this surtax makes the measure regressive and grossly unfair. This has already been pointed out by previous speakers.
These figures are certainly correct. We have long known that the greater part of the tax revenue comes from the small taxpayers and that when large companies declare a certain amount for tax purposes, they hide three times as much, a fact that the other members have not mentioned in their remarks.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, if we were to tax excessive profits, if we knew the fantastic sums they represent, we would realize the amount of currency issued which is harmful to the economy, because it creates inflation.
As a matter of fact, inflation is not caused by those 80 per cent of the population who are in deflation. Moreover, inflation certainly is not caused by those who are unemployed or on welfare. We see the gap widening everyday between those who draw welfare allowances and the others.

Income Tax Act
Farms are abandoned and industries close down because of excessive taxation, and because it is not possible for any reserves to escape taxation.
I agree with the members of the New Democratic Party that this is a glaring injustice. We do not want to take from people all the money and all the profits they make but, under our present system, if we are unable to do anything but tax those who have no money to give it to those who have already too much of it, this is a gross injustice and the government should do something.
If we have inflation in this country and if more taxes and more surtaxes are imposed, we shall unbalance our economy because we take their resources from those who need them, from those who could spend more, who could have a higher buying power, which would make it possible to sell surplus goods.
Canada is faced with several problems, but the most serious is overproduction which has reached such a point that we are unable to empty our warehouses and our stores for lack of money and purchasing power.
We should take some of the tax burden off the shoulders of low-bracket taxpayers so as to leave them with more purchasing power and to enable the manufacturers, the dealers and the retailers to sell more goods in order to produce more. As a result, more jobs would become available for our citizens who would then have a chance to earn a livelihood instead of getting deeper into unemployment and insecurity. In this way, we will not be robbing Peter to pay Paul.
We will not be able to balance our economy, by continuing our present policy because the more we increase taxes, the more we throw our economy off balance. When the population finds it more difficult to make ends meet, citizens accumulate profits and declare less for taxation purposes. We are in a tragic situation and some people say that the government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Bank of Canada can solve the problem of inflation by taking money from those who already do not have enough. The situation is very tragic and must be improved at all costs.
Yesterday, members of the New Democratic party quoted statistics. I will go a little further by quoting more figures. There are in Canada eight chartered banks. Yesterday, the accrued gains of those banks were mentioned. For my part, I will merely refer to the profits of the eight Canadian chartered banks for the last 12 months.

In the past year, the assets of the eight chartered banks increased to $6,647,802,000. Never before in history have we seen financial institutions increase their revenue so much. As for other businesses, they are in a bad way.
If certan institutions are allowed to make that much profit, all the better. Have they not been granted certain privileges by the government?
Many Conservatives and New Democrats voted in favour of lifting the ceiling on interest rates. Everyone voted for it except the Creditistes. Parliament is to blame if so much freedom was given to these institutions. They rule the roost, because we gave them a free hand. And since they have unlimited powers, they are justified in pocketing the profits they make. But the ones who cannot justify their position are those who gave them this sovereign power which belongs to the government and which the latter should never have yielded to such mighty companies.
This is not the way to solve the problem of inflation. The total assets of chartered banks amount to $6,647,802,000 for a single year, or the equivalent of twice the total amount of notes issued by the Bank of Canada in 35 years, that is to say, $3,287 million.
In this respect, we might say several things, but since we have a situation and a problem to solve, in my opinion, it would be logical to withdraw this bill. Considering that revenues may be obtained through other means and that public works are no longer being carried out, it would not be advisable to deprive citizens of what little money they might have, money which has been mostly borrowed at rates of interest of 8, 9, 10, 12 and even 25 per cent.
It is illogical for the government which claims to be a good manager, able to balance the budget of this country and that of all Canadian taxpayers, to favour a few institutions.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Some have said that to solve the problem of inflation, we should apply a control on prices and salaries but it would be of no avail because salaries, prices and interest rates are already too high. This is not the way to solve the problems of our economy which has to be balanced with whatever can be balanced.
Instead of providing our cart with two wheels of the same size in order to keep it going straight, we are putting on it a small
December 18, 1969

one and a big one; as a result, the cart is running around in circles. So is our present system and that does not help at all.
Since our production, in 1969, amounted to $72 billion and since we have consumed for 44 billion dollars' worth, our production costs should amount to $44 billion. Consumers should therefore pay $44 billion and the balance of $28 billion should be distributed as a compensated discount through credits issued by the Bank of Canada. We could thus adjust prices to facts, to consequences and to reality and we could balance the budget of the government. In my opinion, there is no other way to do it.
We would then be the first to fall into step because what we want is not power but reforms, not only I and the other members of the Ralliement creditiste, but all the people of Canada, and it is up to the government in power to bring them about. If nothing better than our solutions can be found, let us try them.
The steady increase in taxes and rates of interest creates an untenable situation and puts the people in an unstable position, in a dismal position, and the Canadian people must get deeper into debt in order to survive. There are almost no families in Canada that are not head over ears in debt. One only needs to see the debts of the school boards, of the municipalities, of the provinces to realize it. All those government agencies are on the verge of bankruptcy and no solution is suggested other than an increase in taxes both at the federal and the provincial level. Other governments do the same.
The people cannot breathe any more. Everything is connected. All the tax suction-pumps are connected to the Canadian body and the latter gets pumped so much that it will soon sink out of sight and vanish. That tax-pumping system will have to be abandoned one of these days. And I cannot see why trade unions and workers keep going on strike for wage increases, for this or that, instead of going on a tax strike.
Eventually, the taxpayers will refuse to pay their taxes. I hope that such a dreadful situation will not develop shortly. Our country would be disrupted. Everything would be destroyed and we would have to start from scratch. We object to this. We want to preserve everything that was achieved at great pains. We do not intend to demolish, we want to build.
Therefore, financial institutions should be set in order and made more practical and
Income Tax Act
consistent. They must serve man. They should not lead us to disaster. We do not agree on that and governments have never found a solution to the problem.
Progressive Conservatives are against this 3 per cent surtax. They have a great deal to say, but no solution to offer. While they were in office, they did exactly what the Liberals are doing now. They never found any solution to the problem. Just like the Liberals, when we suggest to them logical ways to solve problems, they laugh or do not believe in them.
If they feel that the ways we are advocating are no good, they should find better ones.
That is what I ask in the name of the Canadian people. We must improve the situation and administer the country in a fair and equitable manner. We must find ways to enable the people to live decently in an affluent country and when we find that the government is getting into debt, we think it is dreadful.
I know of nobody who can be indebted to himself and yet it is what this government is doing, with its unsound financial system which steals money from the people by levying prohibitive taxes. The economic blood is being drained and therefore, the economic body is thrown out of balance.

Mr. Chairman, it is useful to remember that when a government has a surplus that does not mean it has stored up a big pile of dollar bills which it keeps hidden under a mattress somewhere. In fact, the amount covered by the surplus simply reduces the amount the government would otherwise have to borrow to finance operations and to provide funds for institutions like Central Mortage and Housing Corporation to carry on their worth-while public programs. In other words, the government borrows less than it otherwise would to replace existing borrowings as obligations mature. The surplus in question is already being put to good and effective use by enabling funds to be available for programs like more housing. Because the government does not have to go to the market for borrowing purposes while it has this surplus, it is in effect operating in a constructive way to reduce inflationary pressures.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was expressing my reaction to this critical, carping, prying attitude taken by members of the New Democratic Party. They are always trying to pry things out from government files, they are always on fishing expeditions-

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE RELATING TO POLICY STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: That's terrible.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE RELATING TO POLICY STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
It is terrible because it denies the rule of law. Each Canadian citizen is entitled to be treated equally in the eyes of the law. This means that each civil servant has a right to the privacy of his thoughts, without big brother leaning over his shoulder. This is a subject for humour among members
December 18, 1969

of the New Democratic Party but it is a serious matter to the people of this country who wish to think freely. Free thought is vital to the running of a democratic country. We do not want our civil servants to be victims of a McCarthy type of witchhunt such as caused so much misery in the United States. We do not want that in Canada. We shall fight for the right of civil servants to express themselves freely while they are preparing their reports. We do not want to see this right whittled down.
Doctors, lawyers, union leaders and others in similar positions are allowed to think for themselves without disclosing working papers. What would happen if a government party could not introduce a policy without disclosing every opinion which had gone into its making? It is true some of these reports might have political implications-they might disclose a clash of political views, a clash of principle between people who think one way and people who think another. Why should civil servants be inhibited in the expression of their views on paper by the danger that those opinions may leak out before a final decision on policy is made? This is clearly a case where the government is responsible for keeping papers confidential until it is time for reports to be disclosed.
A recent report contained interesting information on this point. It stated on page 259 that there must always be an element of security, not simply on the ground of national security, when it comes to policy making. The report went on to say that at formative stages in reaching decisions civil servants, no less than ministers, should be able to disagree among themselves about possible courses of action without danger that their views might become a matter of public knowledge.
Surely, this is the issue now before the House. Must these interlocutory proceedings be bandied from pillar to post and handed out to the press before decisions have been reached? If we give way on this point, we give way on a matter of principle and, in effect, we are whittling down the right of civil servants to be treated with the same respect as any other Canadian citizen. For these reasons, I am opposed to the production of these documents.

I hear what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) says, but as long as the Senate exists it is as much a part of Parliament as this House. I suggest there would have been much better co-ordination at public hearings. As a matter of fact, I think we will run into the most unholy snarl in trying to co-ordinate the appearance of witnesses and others at both the Senate committee and the House of Commons committee. However, it is a government decision to refer this matter to both committees.
I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. Macka-sey) who is sitting opposite does not give a damn about the public. Although the people who attend committees do so conscientiously, they are blithely dismissed by many members on the other side of the House who could not care less about the expense and the trouble involved in bringing businessmen here from all over Canada. Many members opposite should get off their comfortable pews. People from Vancouver, Calgary, St. John's, Newfoundland, and Halifax are entitled to come here and make representations. They do not come here for the sake of taking up residence for a few weeks at the Chateau Laurier, yet I think this might well be the result of the rather short-sighted action by the government.
Officials from the Department of Finance will be given the go-around in attending two committees. What they explain to the House of Commons committee they will have to repeat to the Senate committee. It would have been so much more convenient to have them appear before one joint committee. Quite frankly, I do not know why the government decided to adopt this what I call nonsensical, short-sighted approach.

December 18. 1969
Taxation Reform
The last point I want to emphasize is this. The Senators have a great deal to contribute by way of knowledge. Without being disrespectful, as far as taxation and financial matters are concerned many of them have a lot to teach members of the House of Commons. In the same way, we can also help them. Joint committee hearings would have contributed a degree of mutual assistance in this very important field.
I do not know whether the government was stampeded because some members to my left made remarks last June about some of the nominees to the joint committee. They seemed to think that some of these people had perhaps a conflicting interest because there were directors of companies among them. I point out that there are directors of companies in this House. Every member of this House is also a taxpayer and has a vested interest in the taxation system of our country. So why is there this unwarranted and phony smear on a number of Senators who are serving their country in the other place? Perhaps it is because some of them have been successful in business. Since when has it been a crime to be successful in business?
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I suppose one should go around here in sackcloth and ashes and must have been to bankruptcy court a number of times in order to qualify as a parliamentarian, if one follows the argument of the New Democratic Party in attacking the members of the other place who would have sat on the joint committee.
I want to mention the attitude of the minister. He has become hypersensitive about criticism of the white paper. Maybe he has cause to be hypersensitive because he is suffering from shellshock. After the publication of the white paper he boasted that he was receiving words of praise in thousands of letters from people approving of his proposals. I am sure that now the score is reversed, because as an individual member I have yet to receive a letter of commendation. I have not had one person from my constituency or from my city tell me that he approves of the white paper. The letters which I receive are written on the finest grade asbestos.
A number of the people who have written to me have developed good businesses. They are the people who are making our cities, our towns and this country. They are the people who meet payrolls. They give employment to people coming out of universities. They are the ones who make this country go; yet this
[Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West) .1
white paper will hit them like the knacker's hammer hits a steer. It seems to me that many of these business people will have to sell their businesses; they will get rid of them. If we are concerned about 603 businesses being taken over by foreign capital, let us just apply the provisions of the white paper as it now stands and see how many businesses will be sold. They will be on the market; they will be up for grabs, because if there is one thing wrong with the white paper it is that there is not one iota of incentive in it.
My first impression of the white paper has not changed one bit. It contains no incentive. I said this the night the white paper was published. There is no incentive whatever. On the contrary, the philosophy in the white paper is "Save and invest now and we will get you later." It comprises a combination of a capital gains tax, a small business tax and the estate tax at absolutely vicious rates.
Is this to be an egalitarian society? Is this the philosophy behind the white paper? I do not know what kind of dream they think they have, but it seems to be the idea that everyone is to be reduced to the lowest common denominator you could possibly find. I remember a slogan used in the election of 1949 in Great Britain. The Labour Party said, "Fair shares for all". The answer was, "Yes, fair shares for all; fair shares of mediocrity"-and how they have inherited that over the years. Fair shares of mediocrity is what we are headed for. The underlying philosophy of this paper is that you be a spendthrift, get rid of your money.
Let us look at what is being done. First of all there is a sort of hocus-pocus being attempted here. There is a deliberate, camouflaged attempt to show that 750,000 taxpayers will go off the tax rolls. This is based on an estimate in respect of 1969 income tax returns. But when for? For 1971 and 1972 incomes. If inflation continues at the present rate of 5 per cent, of course there will be a gradation of income and a lot of those 750,000 people who are estimated on the basis of 1968-69 incomes will have had their incomes inflated by another 10 per cent to 15 per cent. They will find themselves in the taxpaying bracket. There are no two ways about it. So why say 750,000 taxpayers? That is given as the estimate of the number of taxpayers who will be tax relieved as a result of the increase in exemptions.
If you are to talk about relieving the burden of those people, I say all right, go
December 18, 1969

ahead and do it now. You could give a good dead of relief by increasing the exemption for children, for instance, by $100. That would give interim relief to taxpayers who are finding it tough to meet their obligations. Or, better still, if you want to provide real equity, then give a tax credit. That is far more equitable than a tax exemption. If you have a $400 increase in tax exemption, everybody gains that. The man who earns $3,600 a year has an additional $400 for himself and another $400 for his wife. I am not complaining about him. But the man who earns $50,000-and there are very few of them-and the man earning $25,000 or $35,000 get the same. On the other hand, if you give them an equivalent tax credit, everybody having the same amount, it will be worth a great deal more to people in the low-income group. It will mean a great deal more to them than to those in the high-income group. That is a fairly complex matter, yet it seems to me if equity is the aim of this tax system, the tax credit system is preferable to a system whereby tax exemptions are increased.
We have no complaint about the principle of an allowance for working parents, although this will mean that a few more worms will come out of the can. My complaint is that this provision is to be applicable only to parents with children under the age of 14. What about the single working person who has an aged dependant? How many women in this city are supporting an aged parent and have to hire a nurse or someone to come in to look after a bedridden mother or father? They cannot obtain relief at all. The white paper does not provide equity in respect of working persons with dependants for whom money has to be put out as an expense of going to work. Therefore, as I say, it is short on that point.
I do not disagree too violently with the idea of a capital gains tax in certain limited categories, but why on earth pick on the family home? Why make a person a lifetime bookkeeper? Why place him in a position where he will have to value whatever paintings or works of art he may have? Why should he have to obtain a receipt when he buys something, and keep it? In addition, of course, this proposal will discourage the man who wants to be a proud and responsible homeowner and who would normally keep up his property, not necessarily by spending money on it but through not letting the home run down. He will have a more expensive property as a result, and he will get hit for it.

Surely when the minister speaks about this five-year evaluation in widely-held Canadian companies, he realizes that everyone will get out of widely-held Canadian companies. On this basis people will have to dispose of some of their stock or they may lose control of the company. This, again, will be a deterrent to Canadians.
I suggest to the minister a course of action taken in some other countries, that is, any time you have a roll-over of stock in a resource developing company, there shall be no capital gain tax so long as the investment is in resource development stock. I should like to hear members of the finance committee speak seriously about some of these problems. I am sure they have received the same kind of letters as I have. I think that much of this debate should not have taken place under the rules governing the reference of a paper or a document to a committee, which allow for limited debate only. The minister

December 18. 1969
Taxation Reform.
made this debate wide open when he spoke about the contents oi his white paper. Since he spoke, everybody else is entitled to do so.
In summary I say, first, that this is the wrong kind of taxation system for this country. This tax proposal will deter people from accumulating capital. It will load the requirement for tax revenue on the back of the taxpaying public whom we do not want to overload. They are people between the ages of 30 and 60. Ask the trust companies and the life insurance companies which groups of people in this country save the most, and you will find that persons between the age of 25 and 30, those who are newly married and so forth, have more than enough to do to make the first payments on a home, to buy a car and to cover all the expenses of starting a family. They are not the savers. But people from the age of 30 all the way up to 60 are the ones who save most. After the age of 60, the incentive to economize tapers off considerably.
The people who will be burdened with the additional tax, and some of it is vicious in the accelerating rate of its increase, are earning between $9,000 and $25,000. What is so sacrosanct today about earning $25,000? All sorts of people in the government service earn this amount. Teachers, high school principals, municipal officials and provincial officials earn about that amount. Are they to be considered in the wealthy class? Are those who earn between $12,000 and $13,000 to be considered in the wealthy class, as the minister said? Under agreements signed a few weeks ago, carpenters, plumbers and electricians will be earning more than $12,000 or $13,000, not including overtime. When they earn $7 an hour, that is what it comes to on a yearly basis. They are now in the wealthy class. I ask the minister to speak to high school teachers who in some cases are now receiving a fairly decent salary of $10,000 to $12,000 a year. He should listen to their complaints.
I say that this white paper demands the most exacting examination. The minister has already indicated a number of areas that are giving him concern. He must be suffering from shellshock resulting from the attacks on the white paper which have come to him in a steady flow of letters. He should not get involved in intemperate attacks, such as the one he indulged in yesterday, against the presidents of two or three banks of this country and some others who have been critical. Have they not the right to criticize? The minister assumes the right to criticize any and every person. They have that right also. What is 
wrong with businessmen attacking the white paper? I could almost say it is petty-minded -ness to jump on the backs of people who make sincere criticisms of the white paper. I would like to see the white paper go to committee. I do not want it to go to the finance committee of this House; it should go to a joint committee.

maintopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
The House appears to be in a cheerful mood. We heard Christmas carols as we were waiting for a vote, and we are all optimistic for the coming season. Unfortunately, we have only to read this white paper to lose some of the natural optimism of which we are capable. There are many things in the white paper that would deter the most determined optimist. Although there are in the white paper some proposals with which we agree, on the whole it seems a foolish, halfhearted document. It seems cautious to a fault, and it seems to place the wrong emphasis in many areas.
Sometimes I become a little historical, sometimes I wonder what a new generation coming after us, reading the Hansard of our time, will think about events in this chamber. That new generation may very well live in an age when the name Canada is a forgotten memory, when the historians will say this was a great nation with great potential, which declined because there were foolish men in its government; it was a country full of promise, which had some of the greatest natural resources in the world and marvellous people who were respected all around the world; many small nations looked to us for assistance and help; we were a light that failed. They will wonder why.
They may look at the newspapers of today and see that the warnings were clear, the signal flags were flying, pointing out the dangers facing the country, and yet the warnings
Taxation Reform
were ignored. They will read about a man called Walter Gordon who sat with the government for a long time, who was concerned about the future of his country, who went up and down the country sounding warnings about the danger we were in, and who had to leave government with a broken heart.
They will read about another man called Watkins, who wrote a report pointing out the great dangers facing the country. He made some headlines in the newspapers and then was ignored by the very government that authorized him to conduct an investigation in the first place. They will see that there was no shortage of people to point out the great problems facing the country. Then they will look at the white paper and wonder how in the world any government ever believed that the proposals contained in it would meet the problems facing the nation.
They will not know of our sincerity. They will not know how we looked standing here in this chamber. They will not know how hard we tried. All they will know are the words contained in Hansard. For instance, among the things they will read are the remarks of my honourable, distinguished and erudite friend from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), expressing his great and grave concern for the wealthy of this country at a time when the nation was in serious trouble-and they will wonder why.
I think it will be rather laughable for them to examine those remarks, because if they know anything about history they will recall that there were days when there was no income tax and when millionaires could keep all their capital to themselves. What did they do with it, Mr. Speaker? Did they invest it? There are many stories of how the great robber barons at the turn of the century threw great parties and lit cigars with $100 bills so that they could revel in luxury. These were the days before some of their money was taken away from them. The assumption today is that if we take some money from the wealthy, the country cannot grow. Perhaps it would be a good thing to remove the imposition of income tax from the wealthy so they might continue with their gay parties and good living.
Future generations will read in the newspapers that some of our business leaders were horrified at the reforms contemplated in the white paper. They will read how they abused the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), how they called him a Socialist. They may even read this headline in the Kitchener-Water loo Record of December 9, "Benson Paper

December 18, 1969
Taxation Reform
Rapped as 'Shocking' Blueprint for Socialism." Would it were so, Mr. Speaker, but I am afraid it is very far from the truth. Whatever his merits may be, I am afraid the Minister of Finance is not a Socialist.
The generation of the future will read these things and will think that these business leaders were ingrates. After all, the Minister of Finance has been very good to them. One day he stood up in this House, in reply to a question I put to him about bank profits, and virtually said, "It is a good thing they are having these profits. After all, we get some of them. We are partners." I think the bankers of our country are terribly ungrateful and do not Show the respect that they should for the minister.
When business leaders call for belt-tightening, it is always government belt-tightening they mean, belt-tightening on all sorts of public expenditures, on housing for low income families, on aid to disturbed children, and on hospitals. They do not call for belttightening in respect of other activities in our society, no matter how frivolous those activities may be. Day after day we see advertisements urging people to borrow money and to make use of credit cards. There is no belttightening in that sector.
At times like this I am almost inclined to be sympathetic to the Minister of Finance for the terrible abuse to which he is being subjected. Here is a good, solid reactionary bringing in a good, solid reactionary document and he is being called a Socialist.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext: It is almost libellous.

maintopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
It is almost libellous, as one hon. member says. It is no way to treat a good, solid reactionary and is unfair to a man who is trying hard to be solid. History will recognize these proposals for what they are-a smug, comfortable government making a few slight gestures in the direction of progressiveness.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I started by saying that I am an optimist. I like to believe that Canada will survive the kind of government we now have and that the public will see through the rather obsolete, tired and foolish documents of this government when the white paper is examined. It will be our role to analyze this paper and point out its very serious defects so that the Canadian people will see what they are up against. The minister is trying to keep a leaky capitalist ship afloat by patching it.
We have to ask ourselves what tax reform should consist of. Is this tax reform, or is it a

piece of patchwork? How significant are the proposals placed before us? I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is not tax reform at all. Tax change, yes, but not tax reform. The major criterion of any tax system must be equity. How equitable will this system make our society? It fails miserably because it perpetuates the same old double standard that has always existed in this country. Selfemployed people are free to make expenditures and get deductions not available to those who work for wages or salary. The system for the first time permits a deduction of up to $150 for expenses resulting from employment, but it is certainly not fair enough. It does not change the basic principle and the basic difference in treatment of two groups of citizens.
The white paper should have made a recommendation that the tax free allowance for Members of Parliament be discontinued. I think it is impossible to justify it in this day and age, especially when Members of Parliament are supposed to be trying to demonstrate that our tax system should be changed. I am sure there is not a member in this House who could not make a case for the $6,000 expense allowance, but he should have to make that case. It may be argued that it could present some difficulty in producing bills, etc., but the small expense involved in justifying the expense allowance should be undertaken. I believe this recommendation should have been contained in the white paper. There is a rumour that it was considered and dropped. The white paper should have the courage to make changes. I suspect the reason such a proposal was not contained in it is that the government was not being very courageous in other areas.
Earlier in this debate there was a discussion about the role of the Senate. The hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out that some Members of Parliament have a conflict of interest. I think the day is coming when members will have to indicate where they stand, just as it has been suggested that those in the other place should indicate their association with interests likely to be affected by the proposals in the white paper. Members of Parliament must always be beyond criticism. It is a difficult position and perhaps in some ways it is unfair. Those of us who will be working on this paper must be cognizant of the fact that everything we do will be subject to criticism, that our sincerity will be questioned and that sincerity should be demonstrated.
December 18, 1969

Obviously, any tax system has to raise revenue for public purposes. This is one of the purposes of taxation. But the proposed tax system ignores much of the revenue potential in our society. It still provides special advantages for the mining and oil industries and does not deal adequately with things like surplus profit. For instance, nickel is in tremendous demand around the world but our tax system enables the producers to reap a speculative profit over and above the cost of production. If it were profit based on skill or intelligence, perhaps an argument could be made for entitlement; but it is a profit derived from the natural resources of this country, to which we are all heir. It is our heritage and we are entitled to see that the rewards of that heritage are equitably distributed.
The same is true of bank profits. It is the government's policy to ensure that interest rates remain high because in that way windfalls accrue to our financial institutions. True, we get some of it back in taxes. Their profit does not depend on skill or intelligence; it depends on the gratuitous granting of that right to them by the government of Canada. This tax system does very little to tax sources of income different from the traditional ones. On the contrary, the greatest burden of taxes will now fall on the middle-income group in this country. As was pointed out by the Carter Commission, this group is perhaps the most valuable in our society. It includes skilled tradesmen and many professional people whose entire income generally comes from salary and who do not have available to them the outlets available to those who are self-employed.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that unless this particular recommendation is changed, there will be dire consequences for this country because that group includes some of the most talented but also some of the most mobile of our people. I have spoken to many in the middle-income group who would be reluctant to leave Canada and would put up with a fair amount of abuse before doing so. However, if the tax burden becomes too great, they will leave the country. This is a very serious flaw in the proposal.
If we look at our tax system we have to ask how it contributes to a just society. After all, the words "just society" are on everyone's lips today. Any taxation system which garners taxes only on the basis of income receipts is unacceptable in a modern age. Our tax system ought to be changed and should include provision for permitting our people a
Taxation Reform
guaranteed annual income. We should have a negative income tax, or taxation on a demographic basis, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
We must find ways of redistributing income through our taxation system and put money into the hands of those who do not have enough money to pay taxes. We must ask ourselves how a taxation system will help preserve us as a nation, as well as how it stimulates industry. To my way of thinking, nothing in these taxation proposals indicates the government has the slightest concern for the people of our country. Will these proposals permit us to establish those industries for which the country has a potential, or will we, because of the proposals, adhere to our colonial past as producers of raw materials?
It is obvious that these proposals will mean we will continue producing raw materials as we have been, because they favour the extractive industries. Also, despite the analysis by Carter showing how our relying on the production of raw materials will affect us, the proposed taxation system will continue bonusing the oil and mining industries, even when it has been shown that that is completely unjustifiable.
